title: Rama's one wish
hookLine: Rama's father appears, and Rama spends his one wish on forgiveness

cards: Before they leave Lanka, someone comes that Rama never expected to see again. His father. King Dasharatha, who died of grief after sending his son into exile, appears in the sky in a shining chariot.
He holds Rama close for a long time, embraces Lakshmana too, and speaks kindly to Sita. And Rama, with his father in front of him at last, asks for one thing. Not for himself.

teach.b: Long ago, in his grief, Dasharatha disowned Kaikeyi, who had demanded Rama's exile, and her son Bharata with her. Now Rama asks: take those words back. Be gracious to Kaikeyi and to Bharata.
Dasharatha agrees. Think about who Rama is asking for. Kaikeyi's demand cost him fourteen years in the forest, and it broke his father's heart.
Rama could ask for anything. He asks for her forgiveness.

Hindus call Rama maryada purushottam, the ideal man, the one who lives dharma, right living, all the way through. And old Hindu lists of dharma's marks include kshama, forgiveness, right beside truth and self-control.
Here it is in a single wish.

Then Indra offers a gift, and again Rama asks for others: bring back the monkeys and bears who died for me, so they can see their families again. Indra grants it, and the fallen rise, whole. Now it's time to go.
Rama promised Bharata he'd be back the day the fourteen years ended, and there's no time to walk.
So Vibhishana brings out the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that once belonged to Kubera, god of wealth, until Ravana took it.

teach.h: HE SPENDS HIS WISH ON FORGIVENESS.
teach.b: It rises, huge and golden, and Rama points out the places below to Sita: there's where Ravana fell; there's the bridge, still crossing the sea.
In many families, Diwali is the season of visits and sweets, and of calling the relative you've drifted from. Rama shows why that call is dharma, not just manners.

how: In North India especially, Diwali remembers Rama's return to Ayodhya, and in many families the days around it are for visits, sweets and calls to relatives, including mending ties.

o: the flying chariot that carries Rama's company home
Indra's chariot, sent down for Rama's final duel
the floating bridge the monkeys built across the sea

games.q: Rama's one wish — tap the pairs.
p: appears in the sky to bless his sons
brings back the fallen monkeys and bears

s: Rama asks Indra for a gift for himself
he asks that the monkeys and bears who died be brought back to life.
Rama asks his father to forgive Kaikeyi and Bharata
in Hindu teaching, forgiveness is a nice extra, not part of dharma
old lists of dharma's marks include kshama, forgiveness, beside truth and self-control.

games.q: someone in your family wronged you, and Diwali visits are coming. by Rama's one wish, what fits?
o: make the first move toward peace.
skip them this year; dharma means fairness.
games.why: Rama had every reason to resent Kaikeyi, and spent his one wish on her forgiveness. kshama is part of dharma, not a favor.

practice: Many pujas end with a short prayer asking God to forgive whatever we got wrong. Ask that for yourself first.
Then bring to mind someone who hurt you, not the worst hurt, something middle-sized, and if you can, wish them well in one plain sentence: may they be well.
If you don't pray, just say the sentence, and notice what it costs and what it frees.

wordCard.voice: Pushpaka. Kubera's flying chariot, once taken by Ravana, now carries Rama home, after he spends his one wish on forgiveness for Kaikeyi and Bharata.

orig.note: Sanskrit kṣamā: forgiveness, patience. it is also a name for the earth, which bears everything.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiveness is part of dharma. Rama spent his one wish on it. Tomorrow, the road home in reverse. Day six hundred sixty, done.
